experiment.hypothesis: Standard PyTorch F.kl_div computes KL divergence via cancellation-prone log-space subtraction, causing negative outputs in FP16/BF16/FP32 and backward gradient dead-zones/sign-flips under clamp(min=0) patches. We prove formal floating-point truncation and condition-number bounds for a two-branch 6th-order Bregman-Taylor identity with cancellation-free analytic gradients, benchmark our fused Blackwell Triton kernel against FP32-upcast, torch.compile (TorchInductor), and chunked-FP32 up to V=151,936, and validate end-to-end BF16 KL-regularized LoRA post-training on real Qwen3-1.7B (V=151,936) and SmolLM2-1.7B (V=49,152) models.

analysis.abstract_text: Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization is foundational to modern reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and logit distillation over large vocabularies (V = 32,000-151,936). Yet standard PyTorch F.kl_div evaluates sum_i p_i (log p_i - log q_i), suffering catastrophic cancellation whenever policy and reference distributions lie within typical trust-region proximity. Extending prior forward-pass observations across 36 regimes (forward and reverse KL; FP16, BF16, FP32; eps in [1e-4, 1e-1]), we show this pathology corrupts the backward pass directly: naive F.kl_div produces negative KL on up to 50.4% of inputs and 39.2% reverse-KL gradient sign flips (BF16, eps=1e-2); the common clamp(min=0) patch eliminates negative scalars only by inducing up to 50.4% silent zero-gradient dead-zones (61.8% sign flips); and naive BF16 Schulman k3 (exp(d)-1-d) suffers 100% premature zeroing for eps <= 1e-2. We prove formal floating-point truncation and condition-number bounds for an overflow-free two-branch 6th-order Bregman-Taylor formulation with cancellation-free analytic gradients, and implement a fused Blackwell Triton forward/backward kernel that streams online logsumexp in FP32 registers without materializing (N, V) FP32 intermediates. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, our kernel achieves 0.0% negative KL across all 36 regimes (Wilcoxon p=1.45e-11), cuts FP32 (eps=1e-4) relative error from 21.1 to 1.42e-04 (149,111x reduction), runs 6.54x faster with 80.0% less peak VRAM than FP32-upcast F.kl_div at Qwen3 V=151,936 (32.0x faster than eager Bregman-Taylor), and matches the FP32 oracle exactly in 3-seed BF16 RLHF policy optimization (V=32,000) where clamped F.kl_div collapses into negative true objective (-0.00162 vs. +0.00164) with 99.4% dead-KL steps. Even against PyTorch 2.11 torch.compile (TorchInductor, which disables online softmax on split reductions), our kernel is 1.81x faster with 33.3% less VRAM and 25.6x faster than row-chunked FP32. In real 3-seed end-to-end BF16 LoRA KL-post-training on Qwen3-1.7B (V=151,936) and SmolLM2-1.7B (V=49,152), BF16 F.kl_div yields 13.8% / 30.2% negative-KL tokens and clamped F.kl_div kills 18.3% / 34.1% of token gradients, whereas our fused Triton kernel achieves 0.0% negative/dead tokens and 0.0000 median KL error while running fastest overall (25.1 ms/step on Qwen3-1.7B, 1.25x faster end-to-end with 754 MB lower peak VRAM than FP32-upcast 31.4 ms/step).
findings: Forward & backward gradient corruption across 36 regimes (Wilcoxon p=1.45e-11): PyTorch F.kl_div returns negative values on up to 50.4% of inputs and corrupts BF16 reverse-KL gradients (eps=1e-2) with 39.1% sign flips (cos=0.589). Clamping F.kl_div.clamp(min=0) induces 50.4% silent zero-gradient dead-zones and 61.8% sign flips (cos=0.371).

Even in FP32 (eps=1e-4), F.kl_div and FP32-upcast yield 48.1% negative outputs and median relative error 21.14 (2,114%); our 6th-order Bregman-Taylor branch cuts median error by 149,111x to 1.42e-04 (0.0% negative, 0.0% error >=1%).

Blackwell RTX 5090 kernel scaling vs. torch.compile & chunking at Qwen3 V=151,936 (N=512, BF16 fwd+bwd): Fused Triton runs in 0.90 ms (296.8 MB extra VRAM; Reverse KL 0.90 ms) — 6.54x faster (-80.0% VRAM) vs. FP32-upcast, 1.81x faster (-33.3% VRAM) vs. torch.compile Bregman-Taylor (1.63 ms), and 25.6x faster vs. Chunked-FP32 (23.03 ms).

Real end-to-end 1.7B LLM LoRA post-training (3 seeds each): On Qwen3-1.7B (V=151,936), Fused Triton is fastest overall at 25.1 ms/step (1.25x faster end-to-end, -754 MB VRAM vs. FP32-upcast 31.4 ms/step) with 0.0% negative/dead tokens vs. 13.8% negative (BF16 F.kl_div) and 18.3% dead gradients (Clamped). On SmolLM2-1.7B (V=49,152), Fused Triton is both fastest (18.7 ms/step) and lowest-VRAM (4616 MB vs. 4862 MB FP32), eliminating 30.2% negative-KL tokens and 34.1% dead-gradient tokens.

Version 3.0 audit on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090: (a) Forward KL relative error vs. FP64 oracle; (b) Reverse-KL backward gradient fidelity; (c) 3-seed RLHF policy optimization trajectory (V=32k); (d-e) Kernel latency and peak extra VRAM vs. FP32-upcast, torch.compile (Inductor), and Chunked-FP32 up to V=151,936; (f) Real end-to-end 1.7B LLM LoRA post-training peak VRAM and step speedup on Qwen3-1.7B and SmolLM2-1.7B.
limitations: Irreducible BF16 pre-quantization floor (Theorem 2): sub-ULP logit differences rounded prior to KL evaluation bound all post-quantization kernels equally; fusing directly with FP32 LM-head output eliminates this floor.
Targets full-vocabulary categorical KL (V up to 151,936); sampled-token Monte Carlo GRPO benefits primarily from scalar Eq. (1) stabilization.
Real 1.7B LLM runs validate 3-seed end-to-end LoRA post-training over 24 steps; multi-thousand-step RLVR reasoning runs at 7B-70B scale remain future work.
